Making eye contact with other people
Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation

Threat.value: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Kofi is a 34-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a parole officer in a mid-sized urban county. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 67, and he has come to the clinic after what he describes, quietly and with visible effort, as "a long time of just trying to hold it together." The trauma he discloses is physical abuse sustained at the hands of a former female partner over the course of approximately two years - a relationship that ended eighteen months ago when he was hospitalised following an assault severe enough to require emergency treatment. It is the smell of that hospital - the sharp, antiseptic sting of the corridor where he lay waiting - that has lodged itself most insistently in his nervous system. He did not expect that. He had expected to fear her. He had not expected to fear a smell.

The abuse itself was characterised by escalating physical violence that Kofi had for a long time minimised, partly because he could not reconcile it with his own sense of himself as a strong man, and partly because, as he now says with a bitter flatness, "no one was going to believe me anyway." His partner would attack him during arguments - and in the aftermath, she was often the one who appeared composed while he bled. The night of the hospitalisation, she struck him with an object during a confrontation in their kitchen. He recalls, with a vividness that disturbs him, the metallic taste of blood at the back of his throat, and the specific sound of her voice - low, controlled, almost bored - as she told him he had brought it on himself. These sensory details have not faded. When the memory returns, it does not feel like recollection; it feels like re-entry. The taste surfaces on his tongue. Her voice sounds in his ears. He is back in that kitchen, not in the present, and his body does not know the difference.

At work, Kofi moves through an environment that tests him daily. His caseload requires him to meet alone with male parolees in small offices, and being alone with men - enclosed, proximate, unpredictable - now activates a full-body alertness he cannot suppress. His muscles tighten before he has consciously registered a threat; he scans the room, watches the man across from him for microshifts in posture or expression, cataloguing signs of danger with the same involuntary precision he once reserved for reading his partner's moods. When this threat state ignites, it drags the memory with it - the body's alarm and the kitchen and the taste of blood arrive together, as though wired in series. The sense that danger is present and immediate deepens his conviction that his life has been permanently altered, that what was done to him was a profound injustice that went entirely unaddressed - she faced no consequences - and that there is nothing left on the other side of this that is worth reaching for.

These appraisals have shaped his behaviour in ways that have quietly dismantled the life around him. He has come to believe that positive emotions are a form of exposure - that allowing himself to feel good is an invitation to be blindsided - and so he pushes warmth away when it surfaces, including with his current partner, who has begun to withdraw in hurt confusion. He avoids eye contact with colleagues and parolees alike, keeping his gaze slightly off-centre, which has earned him a reputation for coldness he does nothing to correct. Any situation that might involve disagreement, he sidesteps entirely, rerouting conversations at work and at home with a practised deflection. But this avoidance does not bring relief. By narrowing his world and keeping himself emotionally flat, he forecloses the experiences that might begin to update his sense of the present as different from the past - and so the triggers remain as potent as ever, the memory as immediate, the body as certain that harm is still incoming.

What finally brought Kofi in was a moment at work three weeks ago when a male parolee leaned across the desk and looked at him - not aggressively, just directly - and Kofi felt, with sudden clarity, that he was about to be hit. He was not. But his hands had already moved. He sat in his car afterwards for forty minutes. He is most afraid, he says, that he is not going to get better. What he hopes for, almost inaudibly, is to stop tasting blood when he is just trying to do his job.
